questionStem: Six days after undergoing an operation for a truncus arteriosus defect , an 8-day-old newborn appears jittery. His temperature is 37.2°C (98.9°F) , pulse is 130/min, respirations are 44/min , and blood pressure is 70/58 mm Hg. Examination shows micrognathia and hypertelorism . His serum calcium concentration is 7 mg/dl. An x-ray of the chest shows cardiomegaly without a thymic shadow. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: DiGeorge syndrome is a disorder caused by a microdeletion in the 22q11.2 chromosome, which results in abnormal development of the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches. It presents early in childhood with thymic hypoplasia and impaired immunity, conotruncal cardiac defects (eg, truncus arteriosus), hypocalcemia caused by parathyroid hypoplasia, and craniofacial abnormalities, such as low set ears, hypertelorism, micrognathia, and cleft lip and palate. It is associated with developmental delay. Laboratory evaluation will show leukopenia and decreased calcium concentrations, while a chest x-ray may demonstrate the absence of a thymic shadow, as in this patient. Further evaluation typically includes an echocardiography and kidney ultrasonography. Treatment is supportive. This patient presenting with jitteriness in the setting of hypocalcemia and truncus arteriosus likely has DiGeorge syndrome, making hypoparathyroidism the most likely diagnosis. Severe hypocalcemia can also present with seizures, laryngospasm, bronchospasm, and emesis.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Hyperparathyroidism {Choice A), when primary, presents with hypercalcemia and hypophosphatemia, most commonly caused by a parathyroid adenoma, and less likely hyperplasia or carcinoma. Hypercalcemia presents with abdominal pain, nephrolithiasis, bone pain, and altered mental status. Secondary hyperparathyroidism presents with hypocalcemia and hyperphosphatemia, but this usually occurs in the setting of chronic kidney disease. Pseudohypoparathyroidism {Choice C) is caused by an impaired response of the kidney to parathyroid hormone, which results in hypocalcemia. It is commonly associated with short stature, developmental delay, and osteodystrophy as part of a genetic disorder referred to as Albright hereditary osteodystrophy. It is not associated with cardiac defects. Renal proximal tubular dysfunction {Choice D) commonly causes a non-anion gap metabolic acidosis as a result of an inability to reabsorb sodium bicarbonate. It can be a symptom of Fanconi syndrome, which also presents with hypophosphatemic rickets and growth delay. Vitamin D-deficient rickets {Choice E) presents with hypocalcemia and bone weakening that can lead to deformities such as genu varum. It is usually secondary to a prolonged deficiency of Vitamin D and would not be expected to present at birth. X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets {Choice F) is caused by an inherited inability of the renal proximal tubule to reabsorb phosphate and presents similarly to vitamin D-deficient rickets. It would not be expected to cause such a severe decrease in blood calcium concentrations. Educational Objective: DiGeorge syndrome presents with thymic hypoplasia and impaired immunity, conotruncal cardiac defects, hypocalcemia caused by parathyroid hypoplasia, and craniofacial abnormalities. Parathyroid hypoplasia can lead to severe hypocalcemia after birth, with symptoms of neuromuscular instability and, occasionally, seizures. " , ~ F' r ,

questionStem: An 18-month-old girl is brought to the physician because of a 2-week history of symptoms of an upper respiratory tract infection . Over the past 15 months, she has had several episodes of acute otitis media. She is afebrile . On examination , she is alert and turns her head appropriately in response to sounds . The left external ear and canal appear normal. The left tympanic membrane is bluish gray with visible landmarks ; an air-fluid level is present behind the inferior half of the tympanic membrane . There is minimal movement on pneumatic otoscopy . The right external ear, ear canal, and tympanic membrane appear normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.H: Retraction pocket of the tympanic membrane

correctExplanation: Serous otitis media is suggested by the presence of a middle ear effusion in the absence of signs of acute otitis media. Eustachian tube obstruction or dysfunction leads to the accumulation of serous fluid within the middle ear. Such dysfunction is common in the setting of an upper respiratory tract infection because of the inflammation of the nasal mucosa occluding the ostium of the eustachian tube. Fluid accumulation typically presents with hearing loss, ear tugging, or vertigo. Patients with serous otitis media lack findings of fever, tympanic membrane erythema, or retrotympanic pus, which are more commonly found in the presence of acute otitis media. Treatment is supportive, as the condition is usually self-limited.
incorrectExplanation: nd H. Acoustic neuroma (Choice A) may present with chronic sensorineural deafness or vertigo. They are often small, located near the cerebellopontine angle, and are associated with neurofibromatosis. Fluid in the middle ear cavity would not be expected. Acute otitis media (Choice B) classically occurs in children, often from viral or bacterial pathogens. It presents with ear pain, fever, and an erythematous tympanic membrane with retrotympanic pus or middle ear effusion. Bell palsy (Choice C), also known as facial (nerve) palsy, may result from viral infection or inflammation of the nerve and presents with unilateral weakness of the facial muscles including those of the forehead. Benign positional vertigo (Choice D) results from translocation of an otolith into the semicircular canals and presents with acute episodes of postural vertigo. Cholesteatoma (Choice E) is the accumulation of keratin and keratinized squamous epithelium within the middle ear and presents with mild, moderate, or severe conductive hearing loss, and occasionally with ipsilateral pain if the lesion has invaded surrounding structures. Mastoiditis (Choice F) describes bacterial infection of the mastoid air cells. It results from untreated or recurrent otitis media and presents with postauricular pain, swelling, and erythema. Perforation of the tympanic membrane (Choice G) results in acute conductive hearing loss and would be visible on otoscopic examination. Retraction pocket of the tympanic membrane (Choice H) results from chronic otitis media and may result in hearing loss if the architecture of the ossicles is disrupted. Acute serous effusion does not result directly from tympanic membrane retraction. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A healthy 16-year-old girl comes to the physician for an examination prior to participation in school sports. She had chickenpox at the age of 3 years but has no other history of serious illness . Her immunizations were up-to-date when she began kindergarten ; the only immunization she has received since then is a diphtheria-tetanus toxoid at the age of 10 years for a laceration on her leg. She has been sexually active for the past year with two male partners who have used condoms consistently . She is 163 cm (5 ft 4 in) tall and weighs 54 kg (120 lb); BMI is 21 kg/m 2• Vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows no abnormalities . Administration of which of the following vaccines is most appropriate at this time?

choices.A: Hepatitis B, diphtheria-tetanus-toxoid (Td), and human papillomavirus (HPV)
choices.D: Pneumococcal conjugate , 7-valent (PCV-7); inactivated poliovirus (IPV); and hepatitis B

correctExplanation: The most appropriate vaccine series for this patient would include human papillomavirus (HPV), meningococcal, and tetanus-diphtheria-acellular pertussis (TdaP) vaccines. HPV is a nonenveloped, double-stranded DNA virus of the papillomaviridae family that causes genital warts. Infection with HPV is a significant and preventable risk factor for cervical, penile, anal, and oropharyngeal cancer. Administration of the HPV vaccine is recommended for both male and female patients between the ages of 9 and 26 years. For both sexes, it provides protection against genital warts, with the additional benefit of decreased cervical cancer risk in women. Meningococcal conjugate vaccine is indicated for all children, with an additional serogroup B vaccine indicated for all children over 10 years old at increased risk for meningococcal disease (eg, dormitory, military living). This would be appropriate in this patient who may attend college and participate in dormitory living. Although the patient received the diphtheria-tetanus toxoid (Td) at the age of 10 years, she will need the TdaP vaccine. Children receive a childhood series of immunization for diphtheria, pertussis, and tetanus (DTaP) involving pertussis antigens. The TdaP includes a tetanus toxoid, decreased diphtheria toxoid, and acellular pertussis and is recommended for adolescents starting at age 11 years.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Hepatitis B immunization (Choices A, C, and D) is typically administered to newborns or to adults who previously did not receive the vaccine. The patient's immunizations were up-to-date when she began kindergarten, meaning she likely received the hepatitis B vaccine as a newborn. The Td booster (Choices A and F) is recommended every 10 years for adults who have previously received the TdaP vaccine. Measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) (Choices C and F) is a routine vaccination that involves two doses: one at 12 to 15 months and one between 4 to 6 years. The patient's immunizations were up-to-date when she began kindergarten, meaning she likely received the MMR vaccine. Pneumococcal conjugate, 7-valent (PCV-7), and inactivated poliovirus (IPV) (Choices D and E) would also not be indicated in this patient. PCV-7 was the first pneumococcal vaccine that provided protection against seven serotypes of pneumococcal bacteria. The current pneumococcal vaccine is PCV-13, which provides further protection with six other serotypes. It is typically given at 2, 4, 6, and 12 to 15 months of age. IPV is similarly given at 2, 4, 6 to 18 months old, and 4 through 6 years old. Given that the patient has received all vaccines prior to kindergarten, she likely already has had these immunizations. Educational Objective: Adolescents should receive immunizations against HPV and meningococcus, and a booster for tetanus, diphtheria, and pertussis. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 14-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of progressive tiredness during the past month . She received the diagnosis of type 1 diabetes mellitus 4 years ago and takes insulin twice daily; she has never missed a dose. Two weeks ago, her hemoglobin A,c was 6%. She has no other history of serious illness and takes no other medications . She has had no changes in appetite or weight. Menarche occurred at the age of 13 years . Menses occur at irregular 30- to 40-day intervals . For the past 3 months, they have lasted longer, and the flow has been heavier. Her last menstrual period was 4 weeks ago. Her pulse is 60/min, and blood pressure is 120/75 mm Hg. The thyroid gland is easily palpated . The remainder of the physical examination shows no abnormalities . Breast and pubic hair development are Tanner stage 4. Serum studies are most likely to show an increased concentration of which of the following hormones?
correctExplanation: Hypothyroidism classically presents with a combination of fatigue, weight gain, constipation, cold intolerance, and may demonstrate heavy or irregular periods. Physical examination may show bradycardia, dry, edematous skin, and delayed relaxation of deep tendon reflexes. In this patient, her symptoms of tiredness, progressively heavier and irregular periods (menometrorrhagia), and bradycardia, in the setting of a preexisting autoimmune disease (type 1 diabetes mellitus) suggests the presence of a second autoimmune condition, likely acquired hypothyroidism secondary to Hashimoto thyroiditis. While many causes of hypothyroidism exist, Hashimoto disease is a common cause of painless thyroiditis, which may present with a palpable, enlarged thyroid gland, as in this patient. With progressive inflammation and destruction of the thyroid parenchyma, circulating concentrations of thyroxine and triiodothyronine decrease, with resulting feedback on the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary leading to increased concentrations of thyrotropin­ releasing hormone (TRH), thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), and prolactin. The increased TSH concentration is measurable in serum and provides ongoing trophic stimulation to the thyroid gland. Increased prolactin may cause breast development, galactorrhea, and may promote irregular anovulatory cycles or amenorrhea through feedback on gonadotropin-releasing hormone. Treatment includes supplementation with levothyroxine and frequent follow-up visits to evaluate for therapeutic effectiveness, including monitoring of serum TSH concentration.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Cortisol (Choice A) is increased in primary and secondary Cushing syndrome, often caused by a hyperfunctioning adrenal adenoma, hyperplasia, or an adrenocorticotropin-secreting tumor. Its concentrations are generally not affected, or may be only mildly deviated from normal limits, in the setting of hypothyroidism. Dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate (Choice B) is an androgen produced by the adrenal zona reticularis. It may be increased in cases of polycystic ovarian syndrome, congenital adrenal hyperplasia, and Cushing disease, though is more often used to identify a source of hyperandrogenism in patients with virilization, precocious puberty, or infertility. When increased, the adrenal gland is likely the source of the endogenous increase in steroid synthesis, and when normal, the source is often a functional ovarian or testicular tumor. Estrogen (Choice C) is a steroid produced by the theca cells of the ovary. It promotes bone development and regulates endometrial development during the menstrual cycle. This patient's irregular cycles are more attributable to the effects of hypothyroidism and prolactin than to deranged estrogen synthesis. Luteinizing (Choice D) hormone is produced by the anterior pituitary gland and, along with follicle-stimulating hormone, controls the ovarian cycle. It increases sharply around the midpoint of the menstrual cycle, triggering ovulation. Its concentrations may be decreased in hypothyroidism as a result of the negative feedback from potentially increased prolactin. Educational Objective: Hypothyroidism classically presents with a combination of fatigue, weight gain, constipation, and cold intolerance, and it may demonstrate heavy or irregular periods. Physical examination may show bradycardia, dry, edematous skin, and delayed relaxation of deep tendon reflexes. Hashimoto thyroiditis is a common cause of primary hypothyroidism, especially in patients with a history of autoimmune disease. Serum TSH concentration is generally increased, while concentrations of thyroid hormone are decreased. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 2-month -old boy is brought to the physician by his parents for a well-child examination . He was born at 39 weeks' gestation following an uncomplicated pregnancy , labor, and delivery. He is at the 50th percentile for length and weight and 75th percentile for head circumference . His rectal temperature is 37.2°C (99°F), pulse is 130/min, and respirations are 45/min . Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 97% at the right thumb and 98% at the left thumb and right great toe. The apical impulse is prominent , and there is a thrill in the second left intercostal space . There is a continuous "machinery-like" murmur increasing in intensity during systole and waning during diastole ; it is loudest in the second left intercostal space and radiates down the left sternal border. Peripheral pulses are 4+ in all extremities . The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities . Which of the following is the most likely explanation for these findings?
correctExplanation: A patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) presents with a heart murmur described as a continuous "machinery-like" murmur best heard in the left second intercostal and left infraclavicular regions. Since blood flow through the PDA occurs in both systole and diastole, the sound will be present throughout the cardiac cycle. The ductus arteriosus is one of several physiologic shunts existing during the prenatal period. In utero, oxygenated blood is obtained from the placenta, not from the lungs, and the ductus arteriosus (DA) allows the shunting of oxygenated blood from the pulmonary artery directly to the aorta while bypassing the fetal lungs, which are filled with amniotic fluid. At birth, closure of the DA occurs by the release of prostaglandins and increased arterial oxygen tension. With increased blood oxygenation and decreased pulmonary vascular resistance following birth or with indomethacin use, prostaglandin production falls and the ductus closes. Certain congenital heart diseases require the presence of a shunt to allow arteriovenous admixture of oxygenated blood, for example, transposition of the great vessels. In the absence of such a requirement for shunting, a PDA results in a chronic extracardiac left-to-right shunt that may result in pulmonary hypertension or right-sided heart failure, with the risk for Eisenmenger syndrome if uncorrected. PDAs that are small often go undetected until adulthood because the left-to-right shunt is not significant enough to cause symptoms.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Extracardiac right-to-left shunt {Choice B) occurs in the setting of a chronic left-to-right shunt that results in increased pulmonary blood flow and progression of pulmonary hypertension with consequent Eisenmenger syndrome and reversal of the shunt. This may occur in the setting of a chronic, uncorrected PDA. An extracardiac right-to-left shunt can also occur in pulmonary arteriovenous malformations, which are a characteristic finding in patients with hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia, which typically presents with recurrent hemoptysis and an increased risk for paradoxical emboli. lntracardiac atrial left-to-right shunt {Choice C) occurs with an atrial septal defect (ASD), which is a common congenital malformation of the interatrial septum. It classically presents with a fixed, split S2 as a result of increased blood flow across the pulmonic valve, and a low-grade physiologic ejection murmur on cardiac auscultation. lntracardiac atrial right-to-left shunt {Choice D) may result from a chronic, uncorrected ASD that progresses to Eisenmenger syndrome. lntracardiac ventricular left-to-right shunt {Choice E) occurs with a ventricular septal defect (VSD), which is characterized by a holosystolic murmur best heard in the left lower sternal border. lntracardiac ventricular right-to-left shunt {Choice F) may occur with a chronic, uncorrected VSD that progresses to Eisenmenger syndrome. Educational Objective: A PDA results from failure of the normal, extracardiac embryonic shunt between the pulmonary artery and aorta to appropriately close in the neonatal period. It results in an extracardiac left-to­ right shunt and classically presents with a continuous machine-like murmur. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 2-week-old newborn is brought to the emergency department by his parents because of a 2-day history of excessive forceful vomiting after eating . The vomitus is not green or bloody. He continues to breast feed vigorously but has had fewer wet diapers than normal. He was born at term following an uncomplicated pregnancy and vaginal delivery. He appears mildly dehydrated . His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), and pulse is 135/min. The abdomen is soft, and the patient tolerates deep palpation of the abdomen without crying . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Pyloric stenosis is caused by hypertrophy of the pyloric sphincter, leading to gastric outlet obstruction and vomiting. It commonly presents with non bloody, non bilious emesis after feedings, and begins around 3 to 6 weeks of age. It is more common in male infants. Symptoms may begin with occasional vomiting, then progress to projectile emesis after every feed, dehydration, and malnutrition as the stenosis worsens. Repeated bouts of vomiting can cause metabolic and electrolyte derangements, classically a hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis caused by the loss of hydrochloric acid and volume contraction. On physical examination, an ovoid lump may be palpated in the upper abdomen, which correlates with the hypertrophied pylorus. Diagnosis of pyloric stenosis is by abdominal ultrasonography demonstrating thickened pyloric musculature. Treatment is with a surgical pyloromyotomy.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. X-ray of the abdomen (Choice A) may show distention of the stomach in pyloric stenosis and can also be used to evaluate other intra-abdominal pathology, such as bowel obstruction. However, it would not clearly outline hypertrophy of the pylorus. X-ray of the chest (Choice B) is used in the evaluation of chest pain, shortness of breath, and cough to assess for intrathoracic pathology. Upright chest x-ray is also used in suspected cases of bowel perforation. It is not commonly used to evaluate recurrent emesis in absence of suspected complications, although it could demonstrate a hiatal or diaphragmatic hernia if present. It plays no role in the diagnosis of pyloric stenosis. Barium enema (Choice C) is used to examine for abnormalities in the large intestine, such as colon cancer. It can also be used in children to evaluate for Hirschsprung disease and intestinal malrotation. It is not useful in the diagnosis of pyloric stenosis. CT scan of the abdomen (Choice E) would likely demonstrate the hypertrophic pyloric musculature. However, it is associated with a much greater radiation exposure than ultrasonography, making it a less appropriate next step in diagnosis. Educational Objective: Pyloric stenosis presents at several weeks of life and is characterized by repeated nonbilious vomiting after feeds, leading to dehydration and a hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis. Diagnosis is made with ultrasonography, and treatment is with surgical pyloromyotomy. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A previously healthy 6-month-old boy is brought to the emergency department because of difficulty breathing for 2 hours. He also has had low-grade fever, nasal congestion , and a runny nose for 2 days. He is in mild respiratory distress . His temperature is 38.3°C (101 °F), pulse is 140/min, and respirations are 48/min . Generalized harsh breath sounds and inspiratory stridor are heard on auscultation ; inspiratory stridor can be heard without the use of a stethoscope . Which of the following is the most likely site of pathology in this patient?
correctExplanation: Stridor refers to a high-pitched sound caused by turbulent airflow through obstructed or narrowed upper airway structures, such as the pharynx, larynx, or trachea. It can be caused by illnesses such as croup (laryngotracheobronchitis) or epiglottitis, or by structural lesions such as a laryngeal tumor, foreign body, tracheomalacia, or laryngospasm. This patient presenting with a new fever, tachycardia, tachypnea, and respiratory distress is likely suffering an acute infection involving the structures of the larynx. Croup is characterized by fever, rhinorrhea, a barking cough, and inspiratory stridor. Illness is typically mild and self-limited; however, inflammation of the upper airway can result in life-threatening airway obstruction. It can be caused by viral or bacterial infections, commonly parainfluenza virus. Plain x-rays may disclose subglottic narrowing of the airway.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Alveoli and interstitial tissues (Choice A) are inflamed in pneumonia. Pneumonia characteristically presents with cough, fever, and areas of opacification on chest x-rays. Pulmonary auscultation may disclose crackles, wheezes, or decreased breath sounds. Stridor is associated with inflammation of the upper airway. Bronchi (Choice B) are inflamed in bronchitis, which is a common cause of cough in young children. Typical respiratory pathogens causing bronchitis are viruses, Haemophilus influenzae, Streptococcus pneumoniae, and Moraxel/a catarrhalis. Stridor may affect portions of the bronchi, although it is centered in the upper airways of the larynx and trachea. Bronchioles (Choice C) are inflamed in bronchiolitis, which is a common lower respiratory tract infection in children younger than 2 years of age, classically caused by respiratory syncytial virus. Auscultation may disclose wheezes and crackles. Chest wall (Choice D) pathology may result in stridor in the setting of external compression of the airway from a chest wall mass or an enlarging abscess. Croup is a more likely diagnosis in this patient with acute symptoms. Educational Objective: Laryngotracheobronchitis, also known as croup, typically presents with fever, rhinorrhea, a barking cough, and inspiratory stridor. It is commonly secondary to a viral infection from parainfluenza. Stridor refers to a high-pitched sound secondary to turbulent airflow from an underlying upper airway obstruction, often caused by inflammation (epiglottitis, laryngitis, tracheitis) or structural lesions (foreign body, laryngeal tumor). r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 1-month-old infant has had a 12 x 8-cm , red, raised, well-defined lesion that is lobulated and compressible overlying the buttocks since birth. Examination also shows multiple petechiae and bruises . Which of the following is the most likely explanation for these findings?

choices.C: Impaired tissue growth due to altered vascular supply
choices.D: Increased tissue growth due to increased vascular supply

correctExplanation: Vascular tumors such as tufted hemangiomas and kaposiform hemangioendothelioma are rare in infancy. Tufted hemangiomas present as firm, red lesions with ill-defined borders on the arms, legs, and trunk, often sparing the head and face. They become larger, darker, and indurated with age, although most stabilize in childhood. Kaposiform hemangioendothelioma is a subcutaneous vascular mass that appears as a purpuric raised lesion, most commonly on the extremities. It also tends to become darker and indurated with time. Both of these vascular tumors are associated with Kasabach-Merritt syndrome, which presents with bleeding, ecchymoses, and petechiae as a result of platelet sequestration by the tumor and an associated coagulopathy. Development of this syndrome typically presents with a rapid enlargement of the tumor, thrombocytopenia, hypofibrinogenemia, and increased □-dimer concentration. Treatment options include steroids, chemotherapy (eg, vincristine), and immunomodulators (eg, sirolimus).
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Disseminated intravascular coagulation (Choice A) presents with bleeding, thrombocytopenia, increased prothrombin and partial thromboplastin times, decreased plasma fibrinogen concentration, and increased □- dimer concentration. It can be caused by trauma, severe sepsis, and, occasionally, malignancy. It is less likely than Kasabach-Merritt syndrome in this otherwise healthy patient with a vascular tumor. High-output congestive heart failure (Choice B) presents with shortness of breath, weight gain, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, and peripheral edema, often in the setting of an arteriovenous fistula, cirrhosis, sepsis, or severe anemia. It does not present with bruising and petechiae. Impaired tissue growth due to altered vascular supply (Choice C) and increased tissue growth due to increased vascular supply (Choice D) are incorrect, as the altered vascular supply to the vascular tumor does not affect tissue growth. Rather, the altered vasculature sequesters and activates platelets, leading to thrombocytopenia and consumptive coagulopathy. Educational Objective: Vascular tumors such as tufted hemangiomas and kaposiform hemangioendotheliomas can be complicated by Kasabach-Merritt syndrome, which refers to the sequestration and activation of platelets by the tumor, leading to thrombocytopenia and consumptive coagulopathy. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 6-year-old boy has progressive acute myelogenous leukemia despite numerous therapeutic interventions . During a meeting with his parents to discuss the prognosis and the futility of further treatment , his parents request that the patient not be told his prognosis . During an examination when his parents are not present, the patient asks if he is going to die soon. Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

choices.A: "Have you talked to your parents about this?"
choices.B: "I have talked to your parents about this, and they do not want you to know."
choices.C: "Most children with your condition live a long time."
choices.D: "No one really knows. It's hard to say."
choices.E: "That's not the spirit I like to see in my patients."

correctExplanation: The disclosure of a fatal prognosis to pediatric patients is extremely challenging and requires careful balancing of the ethical imperatives to tell the truth, to involve the child in care, and to integrate the family's wishes along with the child's development and mental capabilities. Legally, minors are not considered to be autonomous decision makers and authority to determine what is in the child's best interest lies with the child's parents. In the case of nondisclosure requests by parents, any disclosure to the child should only be made with parental involvement and consent. In response to this child's question, it is best to gauge what discussion has taken place with the child's parents and to probe the child's level of understanding.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Choice B is likely to create conflict between the child and the parents. It also implies that there is significant information being concealed from the patient. Choices C and D are not truthful responses. While the clinician has an ethical obligation to respect the wishes of the parents, the clinician must also abide by the ethical imperative not to lie. A more careful deflection by asking probing questions is a better response to this child's question. Choice E is patronizing and fails to acknowledge the substance of this child's legitimate question. Failing to acknowledge the question inhibits the child's ability to participate in or understand their own care. Educational Objective: The authority for disclosure of medical information to children rests with the child's parents. In the event of a nondisclosure request, disclosures may only be made with parental consent. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A newborn is examined 12 hours after birth for excessive oral secretions and coughing following his first feeding . The symptoms resolve after suctioning . Polyhydramnios was diagnosed by ultrasonography at 35 weeks' gestation. The pregnancy was otherwise uncomplicated . He was delivered at term with no complications . Apgar scores were 7 and 9 at 1 and 5 minutes , respectively . He weighs 3005 g (6 lb 10 oz). Examination shows no abnormalities . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: Newborns with esophageal atresia typically present with the inability to feed, with associated gagging and an inability to manage oral secretions. As well, since the fetus is unable to swallow amniotic fluid, the pregnancy may be complicated by polyhydramnios. Esophageal atresia often occurs with a concomitant tracheoesophageal fistula (TEF). The presence of a TEF, depending on the subtype, potentially conveys an increased risk for aspiration pneumonia and respiratory distress. Initial evaluation requires an attempt at insertion of a nasogastric tube and evaluation of its position with a chest x-ray. If the nasogastric tube remains coiled within the esophagus, this suggests the presence of esophageal atresia. Air within the gastrointestinal tract immediately after birth and prior to feeding suggests the existence of a TEF distal to the esophageal atresia. Definitive management requires surgical repair. Additional screening for associated congenital malformations should occur.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Genetic testing (Choice A) can be used to evaluate for chromosomal disorders, such as Down syndrome. While esophageal atresia is associated with malformation syndromes, it is not commonly correlated with a specific genetic abnormality. Ultrasonography of the abdomen (Choice B) can be used to evaluate for pyloric stenosis and intussusception, among other disorders. As the esophagus typically terminates in the thorax in the setting of esophageal atresia, ultrasonography of the abdomen does not play a role in its diagnosis. CT scan of the chest (Choice C) could potentially outline the patient's anatomy and characterize the esophageal atresia; however, placement of a nasogastric tube and chest x-ray would effectively provide the diagnosis while exposing the patient to less radiation. Laryngoscopy (Choice D) is the process of using a laryngoscope or camera to examine the larynx of the patient. As laryngoscopy does not evaluate the esophagus, it does not play a role in the evaluation of esophageal atresia. Educational Objective: Esophageal atresia presents with an inability to feed and manage oral secretions. If present along with a tracheoesophageal fistula, the patient may present with gagging, coughing, respiratory distress, and cyanosis in the neonatal period. Inability to pass a nasogastric tube with it remaining coiled in the proximal esophagus on chest x-ray is diagnostic. Definitive management requires surgical repair. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 4½-year-old boy has periorbital and pedal edema and ascites 7 days after an upper respiratory tract infection . Breath sounds are diminished on the right side of the chest. His liver is palpable , and there is 2+ pretibial edema . Laboratory studies show: Hematocrit Serum Urea nitrogen Creatinine 44% 6 mg/dl 0.5 mg/dl Urinalysis shows 4+ protein and no occult blood, WBCs , RBCs, casts, glucose , or ketones . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Nephrotic syndrome is characterized by edema secondary to excessive proteinuria resulting in hypoalbuminemia and diminished intravascular oncotic pressure. This occurs because of loss of normal size and charge filtration of the glomerular capillary and Bowman capsule interface. Causes of nephrotic syndrome include minimal change disease, membranous nephropathy, and focal segmental glomerulosclerosis. Minimal change disease is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children and can be idiopathic or triggered by a recent infection or immune stimulus. Patients classically present with dependent edema in the buttocks, lower back, and legs, foamy or dark-colored urine, hypoalbuminemia, and proteinuria. Minimal change disease appears normal on light microscopy.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Acute glomerulonephritis (Choice A) can refer to a variety of glomerular diseases that involve inflammation of glomeruli, which typically present with hematuria, red blood cell urine casts, and hypertension. The patient has severe proteinuria and no RBCs in his urine, making this diagnosis unlikely. Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) (Choice B) is a cause of nephrotic syndrome that can result in proteinuria and pitting edema. FSGS is commonly associated with sickle cell disease, opioid use, and HIV, and is characterized by segmental sclerosis of the glomeruli that is visible on light microscopy. lgA nephropathy (Choice C) is characterized by episodic hematuria that occurs concurrently with upper respiratory tract infections. When lgA deposition occurs in the renal mesangium, glomerulonephritis may ensue, causing microscopic hematuria, erythrocyte casts, and mild to moderate proteinuria. Membranous nephropathy (Choice D) is a nephrotic syndrome which is more common in adults and can be secondary to drugs (eg, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs), infections (eg, hepatitis B and C), or systemic lupus erythematosus. Minimal change disease is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children. Educational Objective: Minimal change disease is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children and can be idiopathic or triggered by a recent infection or immune stimulus. Patients classically present with dependent edema in the buttocks, lower back, and lower extremities, foamy or dark-colored urine, hypoalbuminemia, and proteinuria. Minimal change disease appears normal on light microscopy. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 3-year-old African American girl is brought to the physician because of a 1-month history of worsening , diffuse abdominal pain and loss of appetite . During this time, she has had a 1-kg (2-lb) weight loss. She is at the 50th percentile for height and 25th percentile for weight. Her blood pressure is 120/80 mm Hg. Abdominal examination shows a firm, nodular midline mass from the mid to upper abdomen . There is pain and swelling of the right wrist. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities . An x-ray of the abdomen and ultrasonography of the mass show a 12-cm midline mass with multiple calcifications . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Neuroblastoma is a neoplasm of neuroendocrine cells of the sympathetic nervous system. It may arise from any sympathetic nervous tissue and is the most common tumor of the adrenal gland that occurs in children. Other locations include the sympathetic chain. Adrenal involvement classically presents with abdominal pain and distention, weight loss, and failure to thrive. Patients may also present with an associated paraneoplastic opsoclonus-myoclonus syndrome. Physical examination may show a firm, nodular mass that crosses the midline and diastolic hypertension. Diagnosis is suggested by the presence of increased catecholamine metabolites in the serum and urine. Neuroblastoma is associated with overamplification of the MYCN oncogene. Histologic characteristics include small round blue cells that may form rosette patterns clustered around a central lumen, with positive stains for bombesin and neuron-specific enolase markers. Neuroblastoma commonly metastasizes to bone and skin. Treatment and prognosis are dependent on the stage of the tumor at diagnosis and the presence or absence of MYCN amplification.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Ewing sarcoma (Choice A) is a primary bone malignancy driven by t(11 ;22) chromosomal translocation. On histology, Ewing sarcoma demonstrates multiple small, round, blue cells. X-rays may demonstrate elevated periosteum and layered neocortex formation. It often occurs in the long bones (eg, femur, tibia) and typically presents in adolescence. Multicystic dysplastic kidney (Choice B) is a nonhereditary pediatric cystic renal disease that results from the formation of multiple renal cysts in utero. It is typically sporadic. It can affect one or both kidneys, with a higher incidence of bilateral involvement in females. The affected kidney is replaced by numerous cysts and retains no functioning renal tissue. Nephroblastoma (Wilms tumor) (Choice D) is the most common renal malignancy in childhood. It occurs secondary to mutations in tumor suppressor genes WT1 or WT2. It is characterized by a large, often palpable, unilateral flank mass and hematuria. It does not typically cross midline and is often smooth to palpation rather than nodular. Polycystic kidney disease (Choice E) refers to either autosomal recessive or dominant polycystic kidney disease. Autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease is a form of infantile cystic renal disease that manifests with the development of numerous small renal cysts that replace the normal renal parenchyma, resulting in end-stage kidney disease. It typically has a variable age of presentation during fetal life or childhood but can be a potential cause of oligohydramnios and pulmonary hypoplasia (Potter sequence) if it develops in utero. Educational Objective: Neuroblastoma is a malignancy of neuroendocrine cells of the sympathetic nervous system that commonly affects the adrenal glands. It may be differentiated from other common abdominal malignancies of childhood by its tendency to cross the mid line and have a nodular texture, along with its association with paraneoplastic opsoclonus-myoclonus syndrome and increased concentrations of serum and urine catecholamine metabolites. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 5-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of a 4-day history of increasing difficulty breathing . His temperature is 37.5°C (99.5°F), pulse is 116/min, respirations are 36/min , and blood pressure is 116/80 mm Hg. Examination shows jugular venous distention and mild swelling of the face and upper extremities . There are moderate intercostal retractions . lnspiratory and expiratory wheezes are heard bilaterally. An x-ray of the chest shows a mass in the superior mediastinum and a large pleural effusion in the right hemithorax . Thoracentesis yields 400 ml of reddish brown serosanguineous fluid containing numerous erythrocytes . Which of the following is the most likely cause of the pleural effusion?
correctExplanation: The patient is most likely presenting with a malignant pleural effusion. His physical examination findings of jugular venous distention and edema of the face and upper extremities are suggestive of superior vena cava (SVC) syndrome, which is caused by obstruction of the SVC and venous congestion of the upper body and face. Obstruction of the SVC is often caused by extrinsic compression by a malignant mediastinal or pulmonary mass, which may be secondary to lung cancer, lymphoma, or metastatic disease from another primary source. Pleural effusions are clinically suspected on examination in the setting of dullness to percussion and diminished breath sounds, and can be visualized on imaging including chest x-ray, CT scan, or ultrasonography. Analyzing the pleural fluid can show an underlying cause to guide therapy. Fluid is inspected for cell counts, organisms, pH, enzyme activity, and serum glucose concentration and total protein concentrations. Low pH and low serum glucose are indicative of increased cellular metabolism in the fluid and may indicate underlying malignancy and/or infection. Malignant pleural effusions may have increased erythrocyte counts or appear grossly hemorrhagic as a result of tumor invasion and disruption of blood vessels and the visceral pleura. As well, Light criteria assesses whether the pleural effusion is likely to be exudative (eg, complex fluid resulting from pneumonia, empyema, malignancy, or inflammatory disease) or transudative (eg, serous fluid resulting from imbalanced hydrostatic or oncotic pressures) through evaluating the concentrations of pleural fluid protein and lactate dehydrogenase.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Congestive heart failure (Choice A) and nephrotic syndrome (Choice C) may be complicated by transudative pleural effusions caused by volume overload. Pleural effusions associated with volume overload are most likely bilateral as a result of the underlying systemic derangement, while exudative effusions related to malignancy or infection are more commonly unilateral. As well, transudative effusions do not demonstrate increased erythrocyte, lactate dehydrogenase, or protein concentrations. Traumatic hemothorax (Choice D) is an exudative effusion that contains increased erythrocyte concentrations and may appear frankly bloody on thoracentesis. It often occurs in the setting of rib fractures and/or pulmonary contusions. Malignant pleural effusion is more likely in the setting of a mediastinal mass on imaging. Tuberculous pleural effusion (Choice E) may be seen in endemic regions in the setting of chronic tuberculosis infection. The pleural fluid is characteristically exudative, with a high lymphocyte count and an increased adenosine deaminase concentration. Educational Objective: Pleural effusions may be categorized as transudative or exudative based on the Light criteria. Increased protein or cells in the fluid indicates an exudative transfusion. Malignancy is a common cause of exudative pleural effusions, with lymphoma the most likely cause in a child with an underlying mediastinal mass. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 16-year-old girl is brought to the physician for an evaluation of short stature and delayed puberty. She has never had a menstrual period . Since birth, the patient's height has been below the 3rd percentile , and her weight has been at the 3rd percentile . At the age of 10 years , x-rays of the left hand and wrist showed that bone age was equal to chronologic age. Her mother, who is 160 cm (5 ft 3 in) tall, had menarche at the age of 12 years . Her father is 175 cm (5 ft 9 in) tall. The patient is 147 cm (4 ft 10 in) tall and weighs 54 kg (120 lb); BMI is 25 kg/m 2• Her pulse is 76/min , and blood pressure is 120/78 mm Hg. Examination shows multiple nevi over the face and trunk . There is bilateral pedal edema . Breast development is Tanner stage 1, and pubic hair development is Tanner stage 1. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Gonadal dysgenesis 45, X (Turner syndrome) results from monosomy of the X chromosome and presents with characteristic physical features including short stature, a wide webbed neck, a broad chest with widely spaced nipples, and multiple melanocytic nevi. Short stature in patients with Turner syndrome likely results from haploinsufficiency of the short stature homeobox gene on the X chromosome. Delayed development of secondary sexual characteristics is common, such as with the Tanner Stage 1 breast and pubic hair development in this patient. Primary amenorrhea is also a common finding. Patients with Turner syndrome may also present with bicuspid aortic valve, aortic coarctation, or a fused kidney.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Chronic lymphocytic thyroiditis (Hashimoto disease) (Choice A) may occur in pediatric patients and more commonly presents with symptoms of hypothyroidism. Thyroid dysfunction is less likely to result in delayed development of secondary sexual characteristics. Constitutional short stature (Choice B) may lead to short stature during childhood and adolescence but usually results in normal adult stature. This diagnosis would not account for the patient's finding of primary amenorrhea and delayed sexual development. Craniopharyngioma (Choice C) may lead to acquired deficiency of growth hormone. However, other accompanying findings are usually encountered, such as headache, vomiting, and visual field defects. Familial short stature (Choice D) is a common cause of short stature, but the child's expected height should be relatively similar to that of her parents. This child is both significantly shorter than both parents and has other findings, such as primary amenorrhea and delayed sexual development that would not be explained by this diagnosis. Idiopathic hypopituitarism (Choice F) may result in deficiency of one or several pituitary hormones, but it is a diagnosis requiring laboratory investigation and would not present with the remaining characteristic physical examination findings of Turner syndrome. Educational Objective: Gonadal dysgenesis 45, X (Turner syndrome) results from monosomy of the X chromosome and presents with characteristic physical features including short stature, a wide webbed neck, a broad chest with widely spaced nipples, multiple melanocytic nevi, primary amenorrhea, and delayed development of secondary sexual characteristics. Short stature in patients with Turner syndrome likely results from haploinsufficiency of the short stature homeobox gene on the X chromosome. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 3-year-old boy is brought for a well-child examination . His mother states that his belly seems big. His vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows aniridia . There is a palpable mass in the right flank . The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?

choices.B: Measurement of urine vanillylmandelic acid and homovanillic acid concentrations

correctExplanation: Nephroblastoma, or Wilms tumor, is the most common renal malignancy in childhood as a result of mutations in tumor suppressor genes WT1 or WT2. It is characterized by a large, often palpable, unilateral flank mass. Patients can be asymptomatic or have symptoms of abdominal pain or hematuria. Nephroblastoma can also be associated with congenital anomalies such as hemihypertrophy, genitourinary abnormalities, and aniridia. The preferred initial diagnostic study is typically abdominal ultrasonography to evaluate the abdominal mass. Other masses that can be differentiated from nephroblastoma include hydronephrosis and polycystic kidney disease. If nephroblastoma is diagnosed, further imaging can be done to further evaluate any tumor infiltration and the full extent of the mass.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Measurement of serum catecholamine concentration (Choice A) can be performed in the evaluation of pheochromocytoma or neuroblastoma. Measurement of urine vanillylmandelic acid and homovanillic acid concentrations (Choice B) is also performed in the evaluation of pheochromocytoma. Pheochromocytoma presents with episodic headaches, sweating, palpitations, tremors, agitation, tachycardia, tachypnea, and treatment-refractory hypertension. It is a common tumor of the adrenal medulla and is marked by the functional secretion of epinephrine, norepinephrine, and dopamine, which cause episodic hyperadrenergic symptoms. X-ray of the abdomen (Choice C) can be performed to evaluate for bowel obstruction, swallowed foreign body, necrotizing enterocolitis, or constipation. An x-ray is not as sensitive as a CT scan and has little utility in the evaluation of abdominal masses. Chest imaging can elucidate whether there are any lung metastases. An x-ray of the chest (Choice D) would be less sensitive for this purpose, and the abdominal mass should be first evaluated. Educational Objective: Nephroblastoma is the most common pediatric renal malignancy and is characterized by a large, often palpable, unilateral flank mass. The preferred initial diagnostic study is typically abdominal ultrasonography to evaluate the mass. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: An 11-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of a 1-day history of lethargy, mild abdominal pain, and dark urine. He had a sore throat and an upper respiratory tract infection 10 days ago that resolved spontaneously . His pulse is 90/min , respirations are 20/min , and blood pressure is 140/90 mm Hg. Examination shows slight swelling around the eyes. Urinalysis shows light brown urine with RBC and granular casts. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism for these findings?

choices.B: Bacterial infiltration of the basement membrane
choices.C: Bacterial infiltration of the epithelial cells

correctExplanation: Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN) is a type of nephritic syndrome characterized by peripheral and periorbital edema, dark-colored urine, hypertension, acute kidney injury, and proteinuria following an infection with Streptococcus pyogenes (group A). The pathogenesis of PSGN involves streptococcal antigens complexing with antibodies, deposition of immune complexes in the glomerular basement membrane, and subsequent complement activation and inflammation. Neutrophilic infiltration of the glomerular tuft can be seen in PSGN. Management of PSGN is supportive and focused on treating complications such as volume overload and hypertension with diuretics and antihypertensive medications. Rarely, severe kidney injury secondary to PSGN may require kidney replacement therapy.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. The pathogenesis of poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis involves antigen-antibody immune complex deposition, not direct bacterial infiltration of the basement membrane or epithelial cells (Choices B and C). Destruction of tubular epithelial cells (Choice D) describes the pathophysiology of acute tubular necrosis. Acute tubular necrosis typically occurs following an ischemic (Choice E) or nephrotoxic insult to the kidneys, which results in necrosis of the tubular epithelium. Granular, muddy brown casts are typical on urinalysis. Educational Objective: Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN) is a nephritic syndrome characterized by peripheral and periorbital edema, dark-colored urine, hypertension, acute kidney injury, and proteinuria following an infection with Streptococcus pyogenes (group A). The pathogenesis of PSGN involves streptococcal antigens complexing with antibodies, deposition of immune complexes in the glomerular basement membrane, and subsequent complement activation and inflammation. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 2370-g (5-lb 3-oz) newborn is delivered at term to a 37-year-old primigravid woman who had limited prenatal care. The mother drank one to two beers daily but did not use any illicit drugs . The newborn appears vigorous and is not cyanotic . Examination shows a prominent occiput , narrow palpebral fissures , a small recessed mandible , and a short sternum . The hands are clenched with the index finger folded over the middle finger and the small finger folded over the ring finger. There is a grade 2/6 holosystolic murmur that is heard best at the lower left sternal border. The abdomen is prominent and soft; there is no hepatosplenomegaly . Peripheral pulses are normal. There is generalized hypertonia . Deep tendon reflexes are present. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this newborn's low birth weight?
correctExplanation: Trisomy 18, also known as Edwards syndrome, presents with characteristic physical features including intellectual disability, a prominent occiput, low-set ears, micrognathia, clenched overlapping fingers, and feet with prominent calcanei and convexly rounded soles. It is the second most common trisomy in infants and is associated with decreased serum PAPP-A and 13-human chorionic gonadotropin concentrations in the first trimester. Treatment involves correction or management of life-threatening abnormalities. Most patients die within the first 6 months of age. In most cases, it is caused by a meiotic nondisjunction, which occurs when two chromatids fail to separate and a single haploid gamete contains two copies of a chromosome instead of one. The incidence of meiotic nondisjunction increases with increasing maternal age.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Arthrogryposis (Choice A) describes congenital joint contractures, which result in impaired joint movement and function and may lead to muscle atrophy. Congenital infection (Choice B) can occur with multiple viruses such as cytomegalovirus (CMV), herpes simplex virus (HSV), rubella, measles, or parvovirus. Each congenital viral infection results in different congenital abnormalities. HSV can cause both cutaneous herpetic lesions and systemic manifestations like meningoencephalitis. Congenital infection with CMV manifests as hearing loss, seizures, a petechial rash, intracranial calcifications, organomegaly, and lymphadenopathy. Neonates with congenital rubella infection exhibit a classic triad of cataracts, sensorineural deafness, and congenital heart disease. Exposure to alcohol in utero (Choice C) results in fetal alcohol syndrome, which can cause intellectual disability and congenital abnormalities such as microcephaly, facial abnormalities (eg, thin vermillion border, small palpebral fissures), and heart defects. Uteroplacental insufficiency (Choice E) describes insufficient blood flow to the placenta, abnormal placenta, or inability of the placenta to deliver sufficient nutrients to the fetus during pregnancy. It can result in a variety of disorders including fetal hypoglycemia, oligohydramnios, intrauterine growth restriction, or maternal complications including preeclampsia, miscarriage, or stillbirth. Educational Objective: Trisomy 18, also known as Edwards syndrome, presents with characteristic physical features including intellectual disability, a prominent occiput, low-set ears, micrognathia, clenched overlapping fingers, and feet with prominent calcanei and convexly rounded soles. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 15-year-old boy is brought to the physician because he is concerned that he has not had to begin shaving . He says all of his friends have begun shaving . He first noticed pubic hair development 6 months ago. He is at the 25th percentile for height and 20th percentile for weight. Examination shows mild bilateral gynecomastia . Genital and pubic hair development is Tanner stage 2. The remainder of the physical examination shows no abnormalities . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: Puberty in boys typically follows a predictable course of gonadarche (enlargement of the testes), followed by pubarche (pubic hair), followed by adrenarche (axillary hair, facial hair, voice changes), followed by a growth spurt. This differs from the process in girls, which proceeds from thelarche (breast buds) to pubarche to growth spurt and finally menarche. In boys, delayed puberty is defined as the absence of testicular enlargement or secondary sexual characteristics at the age of 14 years. The most common cause of delayed puberty is constitutional delay of growth and puberty (CDGP), accounting for approximately 50% of cases, a normal variant. In CDGP, there is a transient defect in the production of gonadotropin-releasing hormone with resultant delay in the stimulation of pituitary production of follicle-stimulating hormone and luteinizing hormone. CDGP tends to be familial with many members of the same family undergoing late puberty compared with peers. In this case, the patient has undergone gonadarche (indicated by his Tanner stage 2 genital development) and pubarche but has not yet undergone adrenarche. Thus, while delayed, the sequence of his procession through the steps of puberty is appropriate and he can be reassured that his development will continue to progress.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Measurement of serum testosterone concentration (Choice B) is unnecessary in this case because the patient is progressing through the stages of puberty as expected. If his puberty did not continue to progress, testosterone measurement could be used to differentiate CDGP from another pathology. Mild bilateral gynecomastia can be normal in early puberty as a result of the small increase in extragonadal production of estrogen relative to the amount of testosterone being produced. Urine toxicology screening (Choice C) would be appropriate if there was a suspicion for drug use inducing gynecomastia, of which marijuana is the most common recreational drug. Breast biopsy (Choice E) would be indicated if the breast enlargement was caused by a nodule or mass rather than true gynecomastia. If delayed puberty were accompanied by neurologic findings or suspected to be caused by a process involving the brain such as a pituitary adenoma, MRI of the brain, not CT scan of the head (Choice D), would be indicated. Neither imaging modality is necessary in this case. Educational Objective: In boys, puberty follows a predictable course of gonadarche, pubarche, and growth spurt. Delayed puberty is defined as the absence of testicular enlargement or secondary sexual characteristics at the age of 14 years and is most commonly caused by constitutional delay of growth and puberty. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A previously healthy 4-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of a 2-week history of mild itching of his head and scattered areas of hair loss on his scalp. Examination shows several small oval areas of alopecia over the posterior scalp with numerous hairs broken off close to the scalp. Several small, occipital , nontender lymph nodes are palpated . The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities . Which of the following is the most likely causal organism?
correctExplanation: Tinea capitis is a fungal infection of the scalp that is common in children. It presents as scaly patches with alopecia, patches of alopecia with black dots that represent broken hairs, and cervical lymphadenopathy. The most common causal organism is Trichophyton tonsurans, although infections can also be caused by other Trichophyton species, Microsporum species, and Epidermophyton species. A potassium hydroxide preparation of a skin scraping will show fungal hyphae or spores. It is treated with oral antifungals, such as griseofulvin or terbinafine.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Candida albicans (Choice A) can cause a variety of infections, such as oral thrush, esophagitis, and vulvovaginal candidiasis. It can also cause systemic infections in immunocompromised patients. It does not cause tinea capitis. Epidermophyton floccosum (Choice B) is a dermatophyte that can cause skin and nail infections, such as tinea pedis and tinea corporis. It less commonly causes tinea capitis. Ma/assezia furfur (Choice C) causes tinea versicolor, a superficial fungal infection of the skin that commonly presents with areas of hypopigmentation, hyperpigmentation, or macules on the trunk and proximal upper extremities. It does not cause tinea capitis. Microsporum audouinii (Choice D) is a dermatophyte that causes skin infections, such as tinea capitis and tinea corporis. However, it is a less common causal pathogen than Trichophyton tonsurans in tinea capitis. Educational Objective: Tinea capitis presents commonly in children with scaly patches, hair loss, and cervical lymphadenopathy. A frequent causal organism is Trichophyton tonsurans. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 10-month-old girl is brought to the physician because of fever and agitation for 8 hours. She has had an upper respiratory tract infection for 2 days . Her temperature is 38.3°C (100.9°F), pulse is 160/min, respirations are 40/min , and blood pressure is 60/palpable mm Hg. An S3 gallop is heard on auscultation . S 1 and S2 are normal. Scattered crackles are heard bilaterally. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this patient's findings?
correctExplanation: Viral myocarditis can present in children with fever and signs and symptoms characteristic of heart failure, including volume overload, chest pain, shortness of breath, pulmonary edema noted as crackles auscultated in the lungs, and an S3 gallop on physical examination. In addition, patients may also present with arrhythmias, exercise intolerance, syncope, hypotension, tachypnea, and tachycardia. An S3 gallop is a heart sound associated with dilated cardiomyopathy and heart failure as a result of increased atrial and ventricular end-diastolic volume. Children may have a viral prodrome of fever, malaise, and myalgia or a recent respiratory or gastrointestinal illness prior to the onset of myocarditis. Treatment of children with myocarditis focuses on supportive care to maintain perfusion and hemodynamic stability, including diuretics and noninvasive or mechanical ventilation if necessary.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Bronchiolitis (Choice A) is a respiratory tract infection commonly caused by respiratory syncytial virus (RSV). Although it can cause respiratory distress as a result of mucous plugging of small airways, it does not cause volume overload, pulmonary edema, or an S 3 gallop. Rhonchi, not crackles, are typically heard on lung auscultation. Endocarditis (Choice B) is a rare disease in children that is usually associated with an underlying congenital heart disease, rheumatic heart disease, or central venous catheter use. It involves vegetations that form on the endocardium or valves and can present with fever, new murmur, vegetation seen on echocardiography, or blood cultures growing microorganisms typical of endocarditis. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (Choice C) can be asymptomatic, may present with syncope on exertion, or may present with signs of heart failure as in this patient, but typically in a subacute or chronic course. Patients may also have exertional chest pain or arrhythmias. On examination, a systolic murmur can be heard as a result of the left ventricular outflow tract obstruction. Fever and an S3 gallop are more suggestive of myocarditis. Mitral valve rupture (Choice E) can lead to pulmonary edema, shortness of breath, and tachypnea. However, it is not commonly associated with fever unless it presents as a complication of endocarditis, and is characterized by a systolic murmur on auscultation, not an S3 gallop. Educational Objective: Viral myocarditis can present in children with fever and signs and symptoms characteristic of heart failure, including volume overload, chest pain, shortness of breath, pulmonary edema noted as crackles auscultated in the lungs, and an S3 gallop on physical examination. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 9-year-old girl with type 1 diabetes mellitus is brought to the emergency department because of lethargy, labored breathing, and seven episodes of vomiting over the past 6 hours. Her skin is flushed and warm and she appears severely dehydrated . There is a fruity odor to her breath. She is at the 75th percentile for height and 25th percentile for weight. Her temperature is 37.2°C (99°F), pulse is 110/min, respirations are 24/min, and blood pressure is 100/60 mm Hg. Capillary refill time is 4 seconds , and capillary blood glucose concentration is greater than 500 mg/dl . Which of the following is the most appropriate initial step in management?

choices.A: Intravenous administration of 20 ml/kg of 5% dextrose in water
choices.B: Intravenous administration of 20 ml/kg of 0.9% saline
choices.C: Intravenous administration of 20 ml/kg of lactated Ringer solution with 40 mEq/L of potassium chloride
choices.D: Intravenous administration of 0.1 U/h of regular insulin
choices.E: Continuous intravenous administration of 0.1 U/h of regular insulin

correctExplanation: Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) occurs as a result of the accumulation of serum ketones such as ~-hydroxybutyric acid, acetoacetic acid, and acetone in the setting of deficient insulin signaling. Dysregulated fatty acid degradation and ketone synthesis occurs as a result of the relative state of starvation created through absent insulin signaling. Extracellular hyperglycemia creates an osmotic effect resulting in the shift of fluid from the intracellular to the extracellular space with accompanying profuse osmotic diuresis and intracellular volume loss. Patients present with signs and symptoms including tachycardia, tachypnea, fatigue, polyuria, shortness of breath, Kussmaul respiration, and diffuse abdominal discomfort. Laboratory evaluation typically shows increased concentrations of glucose, ketones, and a high anion-gap metabolic acidosis caused by the accumulation of unmeasured anions (ketones, lactic acid) in serum. Treatment is through the replacement of insulin, volume repletion, correction of electrolyte abnormalities, and treatment of any precipitating conditions. Insulin is typically repleted at an initial dose of 0.1 U/kg/hour by intravenous infusion. Volume resuscitation with 0.9% saline is essential to restore intracellular fluid volume and lower the extracellular glucose concentration and is the initial step in the management of DKA even prior to insulin administration. Administering insulin prior to knowing the serum potassium concentration can result in life-threatening hypokalemia.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Intravenous administration of 20 ml/kg of 5% dextrose in water (Choice A) would worsen this patient's profound hyperglycemia. 0.9% saline is a more appropriate initial resuscitation fluid. Intravenous administration of 20 ml/kg of lactated Ringer solution with 40 mEq/L of potassium chloride (Choice C) may be acceptable once the patient's potassium concentration is known; however, in DKA, derangements in potassium can include hypo- or hyperkalemia. Infusing a fluid with potassium may result in worsening of unknown derangements with potentially life-threatening dysrhythmias. Administration of regular insulin either via intravenous dose at 0.1 U/h (Choice D) or via continuous intravenous infusion at 0.1 U/h (Choice E) is not the best next step because neither of these options are adjusted for the patient's weight. Insulin is typically repleted at an initial dose of 0.1 U/kg/h by intravenous infusion. Intravenous volume repletion with 0.9% saline is therefore a more appropriate initial step. Additionally, insulin repletion is only appropriate in DKA once the serum potassium concentration is known to prevent precipitating life-threatening derangements in potassium. Educational Objective: Extracellular hyperglycemia in the setting of diabetic ketoacidosis creates an osmotic effect resulting in the shift of fluid from the intracellular to the extracellular space with accompanying diuresis and intracellular volume loss. Restoration of fluid balance is an essential step in the emergent management of diabetic ketoacidosis and is best accomplished with the intravenous administration of 0.9% saline. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: An 8-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of a diffuse rash for 24 hours . She has had cough , congestion , eye discharge , and fever for 4 days . The rash initially began on her face and chest but has spread to involve her abdomen , back , and lower extremities . Her temperature is 38.9°C(102 .1 °F), pulse is 100/min , respirations are 16/min , and blood pressure is 115/70 mm Hg. Examination shows a diffuse red, macular and papular rash involving the face , trunk , and extremities ; there are no lesions on the palms or soles . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: F) Rocky Mountain spotted fever G) Rubeola H) Scabies I) Scarlet fever J) Staphylococcal scalded-skin syndrome Measles (rubeola) virus is a highly contagious paramyxovirus that causes the disease measles, which is associated with acute febrile illness and potentially severe sequelae. It is more common in children than adults. It characteristically presents with a prodromal fever along with cough, coryza, conjunctivitis, and a confluent maculopapular rash that starts at the head/neck and spreads to the trunk, excluding the palms and soles. Physical examination may show bright red macules with a bluish-white center on the buccal mucosa (Koplik spots) and lymphadenopathy. Treatment is supportive. Vitamin A deficiency is associated with severe disease and complications, and supplementation should be provided, especially in children who are malnourished. Complications of measles include subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (a neurodegenerative disease associated with intellectual regression, personality changes, motor deterioration, seizures, and premature death), encephalitis, and giant cell pneumonia.
incorrectExplanation: nd J. Ehrlichiosis (Choice A) is a tick-borne illness with a wide spectrum of disease characteristics, including fever, malaise, myalgia, headache, nausea, vomiting, rash, and altered mental status. It is caused by production of exfoliative toxin by Staphylococcus aureus. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 12-year-old boy falls out of a tree and sustains a fracture of the shaft of his right humerus . He is unable to extend his wrist or fingers . The most likely diagnosis is injury to which of the following?

choices.B: Posterior cord of the brachia! plexus

correctExplanation: The radial nerve is a nerve of the brachia! plexus with contributions from the C5-T1 nerve roots. It courses through the axilla, down the posterior shaft of the humerus within the spiral groove, and then along the posterolateral aspect of the forearm. It provides sensation to the posterior upper extremity and the dorsal hand, as well as motor sensation to the extensors of the elbow, wrist, and fingers. It is prone to injury with midshaft humerus fractures, as it runs in close proximity to the humeral diaphysis within the spiral groove.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. The musculocutaneous nerve (Choice A) courses along the anterolateral portion of the arm and is responsible for sensation over the lateral forearm, as well as elbow flexion and forearm supination. This patient is unable to extend his wrist and fingers, which is more typical of a radial nerve injury. The posterior cord of the brachia! plexus (Choice B) contributes to the subscapular, thoracodorsal, lower subcapsular, axillary, and radial nerves. While an injury to the posterior cord of the brachia! plexus would present with loss of wrist and finger extension, it would also be expected to cause weakness of the deltoid muscle and loss of sensation over the shoulder, in addition to other symptoms. The median nerve (Choice C) courses along the anteromedial arm and through the carpal tunnel to the hand. It is responsible for sensation to the volar aspect of the lateral 3 ½ fingers, as well as wrist flexion, lateral finger flexion, and thumb opposition. It is most commonly injured in supracondylar fractures of the humerus given its course, not in midshaft humerus fractures. The ulnar nerve (Choice E) courses along the medial aspect of the arm. It provides sensation to the volar aspect of the medial 1 ½ fingers, as well as wrist flexion, medial finger flexion, finger abduction, and finger adduction. It is most commonly injured in medial epicondyle fractures of the humerus, not midshaft fractures of the humerus. Educational Objective: The radial nerve is commonly injured in midshaft fractures of the humerus as it courses in the spiral groove. Radial nerve injuries typically present with the inability to extend the elbow, wrist, or fingers, along with the loss of sensation to the posterior arm and dorsal hand. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 4-year-old girl is admitted to the hospital because of a 6-hour history of fever, decreased alertness , and a rash over her chest, arms , and legs. On admission , the patient is obtunded . Her temperature is 38°C (100.4°F), pulse is 120/min, respirations are 30/min and shallow, and blood pressure is 70/30 mm Hg. Examination shows a purple macular rash over the trunk and extremities . The face and extremities are edematous . Fluid is administered by intravenous bolus, and intravenous administration of ceftriaxone and vancomycin is started . Fifteen minutes after admission , the patient becomes apneic . She is intubated , and mechanical ventilation is started . Serum studies show: Her urine output is 1.5 mUkg/h . Arterial blood gas analysis on 40% oxygen shows : Na• K+ HC0 3- Urea nitrogen Creatinine 135 mEq/L 4 mEq/L 15 mEq/L 35 mg/dl 0.8 mg/dl 7.2 35 mm Hg 100 mm Hg One hour later, her urine output decreases to less than 0.5 mUkg/h . A chest x-ray shows hazy lung fields bilaterally and cardiomegaly . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.A: Intravenous administration of an isotonic fluid bolus

correctExplanation: A patient with fever, hypotension, edematous extremities, cardiomegaly, decreased urine output, and respiratory distress raises suspicion for myocarditis and cardiogenic shock. Cardiogenic shock can occur when decreased cardiac output leads to organ hypoperfusion. In cardiogenic shock, dysfunction of cardiac myocytes results in decreased chronotropy, lusitropy, or inotropy. Decreased cardiac output and increased pulmonary capillary wedge pressure result from such dysfunction. Systemic vascular resistance is increased as a physiologic attempt to maintain mean arterial pressure in the setting of decreased cardiac output and peripheral perfusion. Physical examination findings can include tachycardia, tachypnea, crackles on auscultation of the lungs, and an S3 or S4 gallop on cardiac auscultation. Dopamine is a vasopressor and inotrope at increased doses. Intravenous administration of dopamine may be appropriate in cases of cardiogenic shock or refractory hypotension.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Intravenous administration of an isotonic fluid bolus (Choice A) is typically done initially in cases of distributive or hypovolemic shock. It would be harmful in a patient with cardiogenic shock because of impaired cardiac output and exacerbation of cardiogenic pulmonary edema, and it was already empirically attempted in this case. Intravenous administration of furosemide (Choice C) would not be an initial step in the management of cardiogenic shock. Although total body fluid volume is increased (eg, pulmonary edema and extremity edema), cardiac output to the kidneys is decreased. Restoration of cardiac output and mean arterial pressure to prevent further damage to organs is the first priority. Intravenous administration of nitroprusside (Choice D) would be detrimental to this patient who is hypotensive. Nitroprusside is an intravenous, titratable vasodilator that can be used for the treatment of hypertensive emergencies. It breaks down in circulation to release nitric oxide, which in turn activates guanylate cyclase in vascular smooth muscle to result in vascular smooth muscle relaxation and vasodilation. Increased inhaled oxygen concentration (Choice E) would not be beneficial to this patient. Arterial blood gas analysis of this patient shows adequate partial pressure of oxygen. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous
